lesson.title: When the curves move

steps.headline: A price change moves you along a curve; anything else shifts the curve.

lead.text: Price is on the axis of the demand curve. So a change in the good's own price moves buyers along the curve. Change anything else and the whole curve moves: a shift.
“Demand” names the whole curve. “Quantity demanded” is one point on it.

steps.headline: Anything but the good's own price can shift demand or supply.

lead.text: Demand shifts with income, tastes, expectations, the number of buyers and the prices of related goods. Supply shifts with input costs, technology and the number of sellers. A shift right means more at every price.
Substitutes replace each other, like tea and coffee. A rise in one's price lifts demand for the other.

steps.headline: Incomes fall and buyers want 30 fewer cups at every price. Find the new equilibrium for Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 4P − 20.

workedSteps.text: Demand shifts left by 30 cups at every price.
Supply is untouched. Set the new demand equal to it.
Solve for the price, then the quantity.

steps.headline: Incomes rise and buyers want 30 more cups at every price. Find the new equilibrium.

workedSteps.text: Set it equal to the unchanged supply.

reveal.text: Supply shifted left: the price rose from £20 to £24 and the quantity fell from 60 to 52. You solved it the same way as a demand shift.

lead.text: Now a frost hits the harvest. A cause on the supply side moves the supply curve, and demand stays where it was.

reveal.text: Quantity rose from 60 to 90 but the price stayed at £20. When both curves shift right, quantity must rise; the price depends on which shift is larger.

lead.text: Now demand and supply each grow by the same number of cups at every price. Write both new equations and solve them together.

lesson.orientation: Separate movements along a curve from shifts of it, and solve for the new equilibrium after a shift.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A coffee market has settled at £20 and 60 cups a day. Then a fad for coffee arrives.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell a movement along a curve from a shift of it, and solve for the new equilibrium.

recap.keyIdea: A change in the good's own price moves you along a curve. Anything else shifts the curve, and you find the new equilibrium by solving again with the new equation.

blocks.text: You found a shortage of 12 cups after a fad, then £15 when incomes fell and £25 when they rose. A frost lifted the price to £24; shifting both curves together left it unchanged.

recap.nextHook: A price change moves quantity, but by how much? Next: how sensitive buyers are.

questions.prompt: The price of coffee rises while nothing else changes. What happens on the demand diagram for coffee?
hints: Ask which variable is measured on the axis of the curve itself.

acceptedIdeas: A movement along the demand curve
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The good's own price is on the axis, so a change in it moves buyers along the curve; quantity demanded falls.

choices.label: A movement along the demand curve
A leftward shift of the demand curve
A rightward shift of the demand curve

questions.onCorrect: A movement along the curve. The good's own price is on the axis, so changing it moves buyers along the curve.

misconceptions.feedback: A shift needs something other than the good's own price to change.
A shift needs something other than the good's own price to change.

hints: Set the new demand equal to the unchanged supply.
Collect the P terms on one side.
Divide the constant gap by the sum of the slopes.
questions.onCorrect: £25. Set the new demand equal to the unchanged supply and solve.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the old price. Demand has shifted, so solve again with the new equation.
That is the constant gap. Divide it by the combined slope.
That is the quantity, not the price.

questions.prompt: A frost destroys coffee crops and sellers offer 24 fewer cups at every price: Qs = 4P − 44. Demand stays Qd = 100 − 2P. What is the new equilibrium quantity, in cups?
hints: Set the original demand equal to the new supply.
Solve for the price first.
Substitute that price into the demand equation.
questions.onCorrect: 52 cups. Supply shifted left: the price rises and the quantity falls.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the new price. The question asks for the quantity.
That is the old quantity. Supply has shifted, so solve again.

questions.prompt: Demand and supply each rise by 30 cups at every price: Qd = 130 − 2P and Qs = 4P + 10. By how many pounds does the equilibrium price change from its original £20?
hints: Find the new equilibrium price.
Set the new demand equal to the new supply and solve.
Subtract the old price from the new one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 130 − 2P = 4P + 10 gives P = £20, so the price is unchanged while quantity rises to 90.

questions.onCorrect: None. Both curves moved by the same amount, so quantity rose and the price stayed put.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how far each curve moved, not the change in price.
That is the new quantity, not the change in price.

questions.prompt: Tea and coffee are substitutes. The price of tea rises. What happens to the demand curve for coffee?
hints: Where might tea drinkers go when tea gets dearer?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Right: some tea drinkers switch to coffee, so more coffee is wanted at every coffee price.

questions.onCorrect: Right. Some tea drinkers switch, so more coffee is wanted at every coffee price.

choices.label: It does not move: this is a movement along it.

misconceptions.feedback: Some tea drinkers switch to coffee, so more is wanted at each coffee price, not less.
Tea's price is not on coffee's axis, so it moves the whole curve rather than a point along it.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 120 − 3P and supply is Qs = 2P. A new factory adds 20 units of supply at every price. What is the new equilibrium price, in pounds?
hints: Write the new supply equation.
Set it equal to demand.
Solve for P.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Supply becomes Qs = 20 + 2P; 120 − 3P = 20 + 2P gives 100 = 5P, so P = £20, down from £24.

questions.onCorrect: £20. New supply of 20 + 2P meets the unchanged demand at a lower price.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price before the new factory. Solve again with the new supply.
That is the constant gap. Divide it by the combined slope.

questions.prompt: Coffee demand is Qd = 100 − 2P and supply is Qs = 4P − 20, so the market settles at £20 and 60 cups. A fad adds 12 cups to demand at every price: Qd = 112 − 2P. At £20, how many more cups do buyers want than sellers offer?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Buyers now want 112 − 40 = 72 cups. Sellers still offer 60. 72 − 60 = 12.

hints: Use the new demand equation at £20.
Sellers' plans have not changed, so they still offer the old amount at that price.
Subtract the cups on offer from the cups buyers want.
questions.onCorrect: 12 cups short. A shift in demand breaks the old balance, so the price has to move.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what buyers now want. Compare it with what sellers offer.
That is what sellers offer. Compare it with what buyers want.

questions.prompt: Why does only the demand equation change?

choices.label: Falling incomes change what buyers want at each price, not what sellers offer.
Price is only on the demand axis.

acceptedIdeas: Falling incomes change what buyers want at each price, not what sellers offer.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Income is a demand-side factor, so it shifts the demand curve and leaves supply alone.

hints: Who is affected when incomes fall: buyers or sellers?
questions.onCorrect: Income works on buyers' plans, so only the demand curve shifts.

misconceptions.feedback: Supply shifts too when its own causes change, such as costs or weather. Income is not one of them.
Price sits on both axes. The reason lies in who is affected by falling incomes.

hints: Put the new price into one of the equations.
Try the new demand equation.
Multiply the price by the slope, then take it off the intercept.
questions.onCorrect: 80 cups. Price and quantity both rose, because demand moved right along an unchanged supply curve.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price. Substitute it to find the quantity.
That is the old quantity. The curve has shifted.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 100 − 2P and supply is Qs = 4P − 20. Buyers' incomes rise and they want 18 more cups at every price. What is the new equilibrium price, in pounds?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: New demand is 118 − 2P. 118 − 2P = 4P − 20 gives 138 = 6P, so P = £23.

hints: Write the new demand equation.
Set it equal to the unchanged supply.
Divide the constant gap by the combined slope.
questions.onCorrect: £23. Add 18 to demand, set it equal to supply and solve.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the old price. Demand has shifted, so it must change.
That is the constant gap. Divide it by the combined slope.

questions.prompt: Which of these shifts the demand curve for coffee?

choices.label: Coffee sellers pay less for beans.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Incomes are a demand-side factor. Coffee's own price is a movement, and bean costs shift supply.

questions.onCorrect: Incomes change what buyers want at every price, so the whole demand curve shifts.

misconceptions.feedback: A rise in coffee's own price is a movement along the demand curve, not a shift.
Cheaper beans shift the supply curve, not demand.
